decisions.quote:
In two 

well-powered samples (N = 1920), we conducted a close replication of the default effect in Johnson 

and  Goldstein  (2003)  and  in  Johnson,  Bellman,  and  Lohse  (2002).  We  successfully  replicated 

Johnson and Goldstein (2003).
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (note: the Luna triage entry for target_index 0 mistakenly discussed Van Dalen and Henkens, 2014, which is target_index 2). Target 0 is Johnson and Goldstein (2003), 'Do defaults save lives?', Science, 302, 1338-1339 (no DOI is printed in the source text or present in the bibliography metadata cache). Chandrashekar et al. (2022) explicitly conduct a direct replication of Experiment 1 of Johnson and Goldstein (2003) (organ donation hypothetical scenario across Opt-In, Opt-Out, and Neutral conditions in two samples totaling N = 1,920; Part 1 of Methods and Results, plus Supplementary Table S7). The only shipped row (row 2383) is Johnson, Bellman, and Lohse (2002) (10.1023/a:1015044207315, Marketing Letters), which is a distinct original study on online health-survey privacy framing replicated in Part 2. Thus Johnson and Goldstein (2003) is a genuine omitted replication target.

corrected_value.authors: van Dalen, H. P., & Henkens, K.
corrected_value.title: Comparing the effects of defaults in organ donation systems.

decisions.quote:
In addition to the direct replications, we also performed two extensions. First, we investigated whether
the permanence of the decision affects default effects.
In particular, half the study participants were told that
their organ donation-related decision was valid for
three years, and the other half of participants were not
provided with any additional information about the permanence of their decision. We based our extension on
van Dalen and Henkens (2014) who found that organ
donation rates were higher when the option was temporary and would have to be renewed than when the
default option was to donate. Based on these results, we
investigated the presumed permanence (temporary vs.
permanent) consent in Johnson and Goldstein (2003)
scenario. In line with previous work, we predicted
a higher organ donation participation rate when the
choices were framed as temporary (i.e., the decision can
be revised in five years) rather than permanent. Second, we added a conceptual replication of Johnson et al.
decisions.reason: The complete published report (Meta-Psychology, 2023, 10.15626/mp.2022.3108, mapped to canonical file_key c20f9db39f03cdd4 from OSF 10.17605/osf.io/8wd2b) restores the exact reference entry omitted from the earlier OSF extraction: van Dalen, H. P., & Henkens, K. (2014), Social Science & Medicine, 106, 137–142, DOI 10.1016/j.socscimed.2014.01.052 (confirmed in Crossref/Tilburg metadata). Although the 2014 full text remains paywall-blocked and its institutional abstract summarizes only the four default systems and choice verification/adjustment without independently detailing the temporary contrast, the current paper explicitly attributes to van Dalen & Henkens (2014) the empirical finding that organ donation rates are higher when consent is temporary and renewable, predicts higher participation under temporary consent, empirically manipulates 3-year renewable versus permanent authorization in Sample 1 (N = 954), and tests the difference (chi-square = 1.94, p = .163). Under the codebook, this explicit empirical retest qualifies as a conceptual replication target despite the extension label and changed operationalization, and it is absent from shipped row 2383 (Johnson, Bellman, & Lohse, 2002) and sibling target 0 (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003).
